the average composition. Measurement uncertainty is quantified by the standard deviations of elemental
fractions within the cluster (σi), visualized as a red ellipse whose principal axes correspond to 2σi. We note
that compositions discarded during filtering (black triangles) generally lie far from the cluster, indicating
that filtering effectively reduces measurement errors, a trend supported by broader statistical evidence in
Sec. 2.3. When candidate phases with their compositions are provided as input (e.g., PbMoO4 in Fig. 2a,
blue star), AutoEMX evaluates the correspondence between the measured cluster compositions and the      ARTICLEcandidate phases based on their Euclidean distances in compositional space, assigning a confidence score
to each cluster-candidate pair. Because cluster compositions are directly measured rather than constrained
by the reference inputs, any physical variations–such as dopants, off-stoichiometry, or unexpected impurity
elements–are explicitly captured in the quantitative output. These compositional deviations increase the
distance to the nominal reference phase, which is quantitatively reflected as a lower output raw confidence
score (CSraw). A probabilistic confidence score for candidate phase matching (CScnd)–the ultimate met-

   The presented framework also enables the discrimination and resolution of clusters originating from a
two-phase mixture of distinct phases, rather than from a single homogeneous phase. In some materials,
different phases may intermix on length scales smaller than the X-ray generation volume, which typically
spans depths between 50 nm to 4 µm at beam energies of 10–25 keV [20]. In such cases, the measured EDS
spectra reflect the average composition within the probed volume of material [49], which may therefore differ
from the composition of any of the individual intermixed phases. An illustrative example is the (sub)micron-
scale mixture of NaAlSiO4 and LiMn1.5Ni0.5O4 (see Supplementary Fig. 18), obtained from a solid-state
reaction of spodumene mineral (LiAlSi2O6) with Na2CO3, MnO2, and NiO powder precursors [48], and
analyzed in Fig. 2b. The compositional cluster measured by AutoEMX exhibits a centroid offset from both
parent phase stoichiometries and possesses a large root-mean-square (RMS) of point-to-centroid distances
(drms = 10.8 w%) compared with that of single-phase samples, e.g. wulfenite (drms = 2.1 at%). These
are typical signatures of clusters originating from intermixed phases, where the local average composition
fluctuates between the two endmembers. Hence, when a cluster cannot be confidently assigned to a single
phase or displays a large spread, AutoEMX assumes it originates from a two-phase mixture and attempts                   ARTICLE IN PRESS





to deconvolute it into its probable parent phases. This process leverages the fact that multiple measurement
points statistically sample a linear combination of the endmember compositions, thereby populating the
intermediate compositional space, as exemplified by the 2D projection shown in Fig. 2b. First, the cluster
composition matrix is fitted via the non-negative least squares (NNLS) method with all combinations of
pairs of input candidate phase compositions as vector bases, while constraining the coefficients to sum to 1.
For each pair, the reconstruction error is exponentially weighted and converted into a mixture confidence
score (CSmix) via a Gaussian decay function (see Methods). If no pair yields a satisfactory CSmix, non-
negative matrix factorization (NMF) is employed to decompose the cluster composition matrix and infer
compositional vector bases corresponding to the likely parent phases. In the example of Fig. 2b, using NNLS
AutoEMX resolves the cluster into the correct phase mixture of NaAlSiO4+ LiMn1.5Ni0.5O4 with a high
confidence (CSmix = 0.83). Similarly, despite no information on the original intermixed phase compositions,
NMF yields a mixture of Na0.76(Mn0.10)Al0.87Si1.05O4 + (Na0.13)Mn2.07(Al0.05)Ni0.64O4 (excluding Li,
which is undetectable in the employed SEM-EDS system). These compositions resemble the actual mixture
components, particularly in terms of cation ratios—the 1:1:1 Na:Al:Si ratio is recovered as approximately
0.87:1:1.2, and the 3:1 Mn:Ni ratio as 3.2:1. These results suggest that NNLS and NMF are effective in
identifying compositions that are likely to approximate the true parent phases in two-phase mixtures.
   The  final output  of AutoEMX  (Fig. 1h) includes  all  clusters with  their average compositions,
uncertainties, and any matched or inferred phases, along with the associated confidence scores.

function.arguments:
{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a ranked bibliography table for best-practice guidance on creating and using EDS standards for bulk SEM-EDS quantification. The table should have columns: Rank, Reference (full citation), DOI/URL, and One-sentence annotation. 

The PRIMARY recommended paper is:
1. Newbury DE, Ritchie NWM (2015) "Performing elemental microanalysis with high accuracy and high precision by scanning electron microscopy/silicon drift detector energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometry (SEM/SDD-EDS)" J Mater Sci 50:493–518. DOI: 10.1007/s10853-014-8685-2 - 618 citations, open access (NIST public domain). This is the single best paper addressing all aspects: standards-based k-ratio protocol, SDD-EDS stability enabling archived standard reuse with QA verification, dead-time recommendations (<10%), surface preparation, coating requirements, low-Z analysis, trace detection.

Supporting references (5-10 items):
2. Goldstein JI, Newbury DE, Michael JR, Ritchie NWM, Scott JHJ, Joy DC (2018) "Quantitative Analysis: The SEM/EDS Elemental Microanalysis k-ratio Procedure for Bulk Specimens, Step-by-Step" in Scanning Electron Microscopy and X-Ray Microanalysis, 4th ed., pp 309-339. DOI: 10.1007/978-1-4939-6676-9_20. Definitive step-by-step textbook treatment of the k-ratio procedure including archived standards, QC checklists, dose normalization, dead-time management.

3. Goldstein JI et al. (2018) "Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectrometry: Physical Principles and User-Selected Parameters" in Scanning Electron Microscopy and X-Ray Microanalysis, 4th ed., pp 209-234. DOI: 10.1007/978-1-4939-6676-9_16. Covers EDS calibration, QC reports via DTSA-II, detector stability monitoring, time constant selection, checklist for quantitative analysis setup.

4. Newbury DE, Ritchie NWM (2019) "Electron-Excited X-ray Microanalysis by Energy Dispersive Spectrometry at 50" Microsc Microanal 25:1075-1105. DOI: 10.1017/S143192761901482X. Comprehensive 50th-anniversary review: SDD-EDS stability of calibration and resolution, standardless vs standards-based comparison, low-beam-energy analysis, dose measurement alternatives.

5. Newbury DE (2004) "Quantitative Electron Probe Microanalysis (EPMA): Doing It Right and Doing It Wrong." Provides practical error examples, analytical total as QC diagnostic, common mistakes in standard selection and dose measurement.

6. Goldstein JI et al. (2018) "Quantitative Analysis: From k-ratio to Composition" in Scanning Electron Microscopy and X-Ray Microanalysis, 4th ed., pp 289-307. DOI: 10.1007/978-1-4939-6676-9_19. Covers matrix correction theory, coating requirements (<10 nm C), surface preparation (<50 nm roughness), and standard composition requirements.

7. Giunto A et al. (2026) "Accurate SEM-EDS quantification, automation, and machine learning enable high-throughput compositional characterization of powders" Nat Commun. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-76633-x. Demonstrates one-time standard measurement per element enabling permanent reference sets for all future analyses on same instrument; validates 5-10% RDEV accuracy across 74 samples.

8. ASTM E1508-12a (reapproved 2019) "Standard Guide for Quantitative Analysis by Energy-Dispersive Spectroscopy using the SEM" - Formal consensus document covering standards selection, surface preparation, and analytical procedures.

9. ISO 22309:2011 "Microbeam analysis — Quantitative analysis using energy-dispersive spectrometry (EDS) for elements with an atomic number of 11 (Na) or above" - International standard for quantitative EDS analysis.

10. Jarosewich E, Nelen JA, Norberg JA (1980) "Reference Samples for Electron Microprobe Analysis" Geostandards Newsletter 4:43-47. DOI: 10.1111/j.1751-908X.1980.tb00273.x. Classic reference establishing Smithsonian microbeam mineral standards widely used as secondary standards.

11. Rinaldi R, Llovet X (2015) "Electron Probe Microanalysis: A Review of the Past, Present, and Future" Microsc Microanal 21:1053-1069. DOI: 10.1017/S1431927615000409. Comprehensive review of EPMA development including standards, homogeneity requirements, and future directions."}

function.arguments:
{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a table summarizing what must be IDENTICAL, what must be RECORDED, and what must be in an ACCEPTABLE RANGE for standards-based SEM-EDS k-ratio quantification when reusing archived standards. This addresses the user's question #4.

Columns: Parameter Category, Parameter, Requirement, Notes/Rationale

MUST BE IDENTICAL between standard and unknown:
- Beam energy (E0) - Must match exactly. Verify by Duane-Hunt limit check.
- EDS detector - Same physical detector
- Pulse process time / time constant - Must be same setting. Controls resolution and throughput.
- Detector-to-specimen distance (solid angle) - Fixed by detector flange typically, but verify working distance is same
- Takeoff angle / detector elevation angle - Fixed by geometry; must match
- Specimen tilt angle - Ideally 0° for both; must be identical if tilted
- Conductive coating scheme - Same material (C), same nominal thickness (<10 nm), especially critical at low kV (5 kV)

MUST BE RECORDED (but need not be identical):
- Probe current (beam current) - Must be measured (Faraday cup or picoammeter) and recorded for each session; used for dose calculation but cancels in k-ratio if dose is properly tracked
- Live time - Must be accurately recorded by dead-time-corrected clock; used with beam current to compute dose
- Acquisition date/time - For traceability and QC tracking

MUST BE IN AN ACCEPTABLE RANGE (but need not be identical):
- Dead time - ≤10% recommended for SDD-EDS quantitative work; ≤5% for trace analysis; need NOT match between standard and unknown
- Input count rate / output count rate - Should produce acceptable dead time; avoid very high rates that cause excessive coincidence
- Spectrum integrated counts - Should be sufficient for desired precision (typically >1 million for major, >10 million for minor/trace)
- Surface roughness - Must be below 50 nm RMS for low-energy photons (<1 keV), below 100 nm RMS for higher energies"}

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Parameter Category | Parameter | Requirement | Notes/Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Must be identical | Beam energy (E0) | Exact same set point for standard and unknown | k-ratio protocol assumes identical excitation conditions; verify actual beam energy from the continuum end point/Duane-Hunt limit as a QC check, especially when reusing archived standards (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000007) |
| Must be identical | EDS detector | Same physical detector | Archived standards are detector-specific because window transmission, solid angle, and response function are part of the measured standard spectrum (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000010) |
| Must be identical | Pulse process time / time constant | Same setting | Time constant controls resolution, peak shape, and throughput; archived standards are only valid if the same processing conditions are used (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000028) |
| Must be identical | Detector-to-specimen distance / effective solid angle | Same geometry; in practice maintain the same working distance and detector position | Measured intensity scales with solid angle; even if the detector flange is fixed, working distance and specimen height must reproduce the archived-standard geometry (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000031) |
| Must be identical | Takeoff angle / detector elevation geometry | Same geometry | X-ray absorption corrections depend on emergence angle, so archived standards should only be reused under the same takeoff geometry (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000031) |
| Must be identical | Specimen tilt angle | Ideally 0° for both; if tilted, tilt must match exactly | Tilt changes path length and absorption; low-tilt, flat geometry is strongly preferred for quantitative work (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000031) |
| Must be identical | Conductive coating scheme | Same coating material and nominal thickness | Coating differences can shift analytical totals and bias k-ratios; for low-kV work (≈5 keV and below) matching coating thickness becomes especially important (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033) |
| Must be recorded | Probe current (beam current) | Measure or otherwise normalize and record for each session | Dose = beam current × live time; absolute current is preferred via Faraday cup/picoammeter, but if unavailable a QC-standard intensity can be used to normalize dose within a verified workflow (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007) |
| Must be recorded | Live time | Record accurately using the dead-time-corrected live-time clock | Dose normalization requires live time, not just real time; intensity should scale linearly with effective dose (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000026) |
| Must be recorded | Acquisition date/time and session metadata | Record for traceability | Needed for archived-standard provenance, long-term QC charts, and troubleshooting drift or maintenance events (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010) |
| Must be in an acceptable range | Dead time | Keep low; about ≤10% recommended for SDD quantitative work, and more conservative for trace work | Dead time does **not** need to be identical between standard and unknown; it must simply stay in a regime where coincidence/pile-up artifacts are negligible and correction remains reliable (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028) |
| Must be in an acceptable range | Input/output count rate | Any rate that preserves stable calibration/resolution and acceptable dead time | Modern SDD systems tolerate high throughput, but very high count rates increase coincidence artifacts; choose rates by detector behavior, not by forcing equality between standard and unknown (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000027) |
| Must be in an acceptable range | Spectrum integrated counts | Sufficient for the target precision | High-count spectra are essential for minor/trace work and robust peak fitting; examples in the literature range from millions to tens of millions of counts depending on problem difficulty (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000025) |
| Must be in an acceptable range | Surface roughness / polish quality | Better than ~100 nm RMS generally; better than ~50 nm RMS for low-energy photons (<1 keV) | Surface topography changes absorption and geometry; low-kV Al/Si/Mg K analysis is especially surface-sensitive, so final polish quality matters directly to k-ratio validity (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032) |


*Table: This table separates conditions that must be strictly matched from those that only need documentation or control within acceptable limits when reusing archived bulk SEM-EDS standards. It is useful for building a reusable per-voltage standards library without imposing unnecessary constraints such as identical dead time.*

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.

Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at

Double-check your answer:

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: We perform standards-based k-ratio quantification of bulk samples by SEM-EDS (NIST DTSA-II; EDAX Octane Plus SDD on a Thermo Fisher Apreo SEM). Current case: laser powder bed fusion AlSi10Mg (Al ~89 wt%, Si ~10, Mg 0.2-1) analyzed at 5 kV using Al Ka, Si Ka, Mg Ka, with planned standards pure Al, Si wafer, and MgO. The lab uses fixed accelerating-voltage set points of 5, 10, 15, and 20 kV and wants to build a reusable per-voltage standards library.

Find and rank published best-practice guidance for CREATING and USING EDS standards for bulk SEM-EDS quantification (exclude TEM entirely: no Cliff-Lorimer, no zeta factors, no thin-film methods). Address specifically:

1. Temporal validity and reuse: must standard spectra be acquired in the same session as the unknown, or can archived standard spectra be reused across days/months/years on the same detector at the same beam energy and pulse process time? Cite quantitative evidence for long-term stability of SDD-EDS systems (energy calibration drift, resolution drift, detector efficiency drift, counts per unit dose over months/years) that supports or limits archived-standard reuse - e.g., NIST work by Ritchie, Newbury and colleagues demonstrating SDD-EDS reproducibility over long periods.

2. Per-session quality control when reusing archived standards: recommended re-verification protocol (energy calibration zero/gain check, resolution/FWHM check, counts-per-nA-second check on a QC material, Duane-Hunt limit check for true beam energy), tolerances, and drift-correction practices.

3. Dose normalization: requirements for probe-current measurement (Faraday cup, picoammeter) when reusing archived standards; how beam-current measurement error and drift propagate into k-ratios and concentrations; accepted practices when an instrument cannot measure absolute probe current (e.g., in-session standards, or normalizing dose via a QC standard count rate).

4. What must be IDENTICAL between standard and unknown acquisitions (detector, geometry/working distance/takeoff/tilt, beam energy, pulse process/shaping time, coating scheme) versus what only needs to be RECORDED (probe current, live time) versus what only needs to be IN AN ACCEPTABLE RANGE (dead time, count rate) - including recommended dead-time limits for quantitative and trace work and the role of pulse pile-up. Explicitly address the common misconception that dead time must be identical between standard and unknown.

5. Creating standards: choice of materials (pure elements vs stoichiometric compounds vs matrix-matched or type standards), homogeneity requirements and verification, surface preparation and polishing, conductive coating matching, mounting; special considerations at low beam energy (5 kV) where surface films dominate; care and storage of physical standard blocks between sessions (oxidation of metals, hydration of MgO, repolishing intervals).

6. Formal consensus documents and classics: ASTM E1508 (Standard Guide for Quantitative Analysis by Energy-Dispersive Spectroscopy), ISO 22309, ISO 15632 (EDS performance parameters), and classic standard-material references (e.g., Jarosewich, Nelen and Norberg 1980 Smithsonian microbeam reference samples; Marinenko's standards chapter in Electron Probe Quantitation 1991; Ritchie/Newbury/Davis 2012 on SDD-EDS k-ratio precision at WDS levels).

Deliverables: identify ONE primary recommended paper that best answers "best practices for creating and using EDS standards, including whether archived standards may be reused across sessions," then a supporting list (5-10 items) with one-sentence annotations, complete citations with DOIs, and open-access links where available. Prefer sources with measured evidence over convention.

Abstract:
An oven microwave was established for synthesis of zinc oxide nanoparticles using Sargassum sp. and Padina sp. extract and 0.1 M ZnCl2 solution as a precursor. The ZnO nanoparticles had been characterized such as chemical structure by Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, particle size distribution with Particle Size Analyzer (PSA), Scanning Electron Microscopy-Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (SEMEDS) and crystalline properties with X-ray diffraction (XRD). The result showed that FTIR spectra revealed the involvement of hydroxyl groups and sulfate polysaccharide in the formation of ZnO NPs and protein was involved in stabilizing. PSA analysis showed that the size ranged of ZnO NPs extract Sargassum sp. synthesized 351,14 and 1.336.19 nm for extract Padina sp. The particle size distribution was homogeneous but their size hadn’t met the size of nanometers. The range of %mass elements Zn and O ZnO extract Sargassum sp. and Padina sp. synthesized didn’t approach standard ZnO. The crystallinity properties showed only ZnO extract of Padina sp. synthesized which had a peak with an angle value of 2θ was almost equal to standard ZnO and after confirmed to Match program! 3 crystal structure ZnO synthesized wasn’t imperfect hexagonal wurtzite. Ovens microwave could be used to synthesize ZnO from Padina sp. extract but it was still necessary to develop a method so that ZnO could be obtained with nanoparticle size and ideal hexagonal wurtzit structure.

Abstract:
Abstract Although targeting TfR1 to deliver oligonucleotides to skeletal muscle has been demonstrated in rodents, effectiveness and pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PKPD) properties remained unknown in higher species. We developed antibody–oligonucleotide conjugates (AOCs) towards mice or monkeys utilizing anti-TfR1 monoclonal antibodies (αTfR1) conjugated to various classes of oligonucleotides (siRNA, ASOs and PMOs). αTfR1 AOCs delivered oligonucleotides to muscle tissue in both species. In mice, αTfR1 AOCs achieved a > 15-fold higher concentration to muscle tissue than unconjugated siRNA. A single dose of an αTfR1 conjugated to an siRNA against Ssb mRNA produced > 75% Ssb mRNA reduction in mice and monkeys, and mRNA silencing was greatest in skeletal and cardiac (striated) muscle with minimal to no activity in other major organs. In mice the EC50 for Ssb mRNA reduction in skeletal muscle was >75-fold less than in systemic tissues. Oligonucleotides conjugated to control antibodies or cholesterol produced no mRNA reduction or were 10-fold less potent, respectively. Tissue PKPD of AOCs demonstrated mRNA silencing activity primarily driven by receptor-mediated delivery in striated muscle for siRNA oligonucleotides. In mice, we show that AOC-mediated delivery is operable across various oligonucleotide modalities. AOC PKPD properties translated to higher species, providing promise for a new class of oligonucleotide therapeutics.

Abstract:
Knowledge of dynamic niche-specific interactions between single microbes and host cells is essential to understand infectious disease progression. However, advances in this field have been hampered by the inherent conflict between the technical requirements for high-resolution live-cell imaging on the one hand and conditions that best mimic physiological infection niche parameters on the other. ABSTRACT Interactions between individual pathogenic microbes and host tissues involve fast and dynamic processes that ultimately impact the outcome of infection. Using live-cell microscopy, these dynamics can be visualized to study, e.g., microbe motility, binding and invasion of host cells, and intrahost-cell survival. Such methodology typically employs confocal imaging of fluorescent tags in tumor-derived cell line infections on glass. This allows high-definition imaging but poorly reflects the host tissue’s physiological architecture and may result in artifacts. We developed a method for live-cell imaging of microbial infection dynamics on human adult stem cell-derived intestinal epithelial cell (IEC) layers. These IEC layers are grown in apical imaging chambers, optimized for physiological cell arrangement and fast, but gentle, differential interference contrast (DIC) imaging. This allows subsecond visualization of both microbial and epithelial surface ultrastructure at high resolution without using fluorescent reporters. We employed this technology to probe the behavior of two model pathogens, Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium and Giardia intestinalis, at the intestinal epithelial surface. Our results reveal pathogen-specific swimming patterns on the epithelium and show that Salmonella lingers on the IEC surface for prolonged periods before host cell invasion, while Giardia uses circular swimming with intermittent attachments to scout for stable adhesion sites. The method even permits tracking of individual Giardia flagella, demonstrating that active flagellar beating and attachment to the IEC surface are not mutually exclusive. This work describes a generalizable and relatively inexpensive approach to resolving dynamic pathogen-IEC layer interactions, applicable even to genetically nontractable microorganisms. IMPORTANCE Knowledge of dynamic niche-specific interactions between single microbes and host cells is essential to understand infectious disease progression. However, advances in this field have been hampered by the inherent conflict between the technical requirements for high-resolution live-cell imaging on the one hand and conditions that best mimic physiological infection niche parameters on the other. Toward bridging this divide, we present a methodology for differential interference contrast (DIC) imaging of pathogen interactions at the apical surface of enteroid-derived intestinal epithelia, providing both high spatial and temporal resolution. This alleviates the need for fluorescent reporters in live-cell imaging and provides dynamic information about microbe interactions with a nontransformed, confluent, polarized, and microvilliated human gut epithelium. Using this methodology, we uncover previously unrecognized stages of Salmonella and Giardia infection cycles at the epithelial surface.

Abstract:
The desalination of seawater using reverse osmosis membranes is an attractive solution to global freshwater scarcity. However, membrane performance is reduced by (bio)fouling. Membrane autopsies are essential for identifying the type of fouling material, and applying corrective measures to minimize membrane fouling. Information from full-scale membrane autopsies guiding improved plant operations is scant in the formal literature. In this case-study, a reverse osmosis membrane from a full-scale seawater desalination plant with a feed channel pressure drop increase of about 218% over the pressure vessel was autopsied. The simultaneous determination of microbial cells, ATP, and total organic carbon (TOC) abundances per membrane area allowed estimating the contributions of biofouling and organic fouling. The abundance of microbial cells determined by flow cytometry (up to 7 × 108 cells/cm2), and ATP (up to 21,000 pg/cm2) as well as TOC (up to 98 μg/cm2) were homogeneously distributed on the membrane. Inorganic fouling was also measured, and followed a similar coverage distribution to that of biofouling. Iron (∼150 μg/cm2, estimated by ICP-MS) was the main inorganic foulant. ATR-FTIR spectra supported that membrane fouling was both organic/biological and inorganic. High-resolution SEM-EDS imaging of cross-sectioned membranes allowed assessing the thickness of the fouling layer (up to 20 μm) and its elemental composition. Imaging results further supported the results of homogeneous fouling coverage. Moreover, imaging revealed both zones with and without compression of the polysulfone membrane layer, suggesting that the stress due to operating pressure was heterogeneous. The procedure for this membrane autopsy provided a reasonable overview of the diverse contributors of fouling and might be a starting point to building a consensus autopsy protocol. Next, it would be valuable to build a RO membrane autopsy database, which can be used as a guidance and diagnostic tool to improve the management and operation of RO desalination plants.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
          <jats:p>The application of X-ray methods (using conventional sources or synchrotron radiation) for investigating degradation phenomena in paintings has significantly increased in the last two decades. This rise is due to their ability to provide spatially resolved elemental, molecular, and structural information from the macroscopic to the nanoscopic levels. This review will focus on the application of latest-generation X-ray techniques, including X-ray fluorescence (XRF), X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), and X-ray diffraction (XRD), to study the alteration processes of pigments in paintings. The first part outlines the fundamentals of XRF, XAS, and XRD techniques and then describes the corresponding instrumental set-ups used for non-invasive macro-scale mapping of paintings and synchrotron radiation-based X-ray analysis of paint micro-samples. Subsequent sections will cover advancements in X-ray data analysis software, workflow management systems, Open Science and FAIR data initiatives, alongside practical aspects of sample preparation and issues concerning X-ray-induced damage to paints. The final section will review degradation phenomena resulting from chemical changes of selected classes of pigments. This will involve describing key findings obtained from paintings, related micro-samples, and artificially aged paint mock-ups. The outcomes discussed in this review highlight their crucial role in developing effective monitoring and preventive conservation strategies for artworks highly susceptible to degradation within heritage sites and museums.</jats:p>

M. and Scott, John Henry J. and Joy, David C.", title = "Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectrometry: Physical Principles and User-Selected Parameters", year = "2018", journal = "ArXiv", pages = "209-234", doi = "10.1007/978-1-4939-6676-9\_16", url = "https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4939-6676-9\_16", month = "Nov", publisher = "Springer New York" } Abstract: As illustrated in Fig. 16.1, the physical basis of energy dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS) with a semiconductor detector begins with photoelectric absorption of an X-ray photon in the active volume of the semiconductor (Si). The entire energy of the photon is transferred to a bound inner shell atomic electron, which is ejected with kinetic energy equal to the photon energy minus the shell ionization energy (binding energy), 1.838 keV for the Si K-shell and 0.098 keV for the Si L-shell. The ejected photoelectron undergoes inelastic scattering within the Si crystal. One of the consequences of the energy loss is the promotion of bound outer shell valence electrons to the conduction band of the semiconductor, leaving behind positively charged “holes” in the valence band. In the conduction band, the free electrons can move in response to a potential applied between the entrance surface electrode and the back surface electrode across the thickness of the Si crystal, while the positive holes in the conduction band drift in the opposite direction, resulting in the collection of electrons at the anode on the back surface of the EDS detector. This charge generation process requires approximately 3.6 eV per electron hole pair, so that the number of charge carriers is proportional to the original photon energy, Ep: $$ n={E}_p/3.6\ eV $$ For a Mn K-L3 photon with an energy of 5.895 keV, approximately 1638 electron–hole pairs are created, comprising a charge of 2.6 × 10−16 coulombs. Because the detector can respond to any photon energy from a threshold of approximately 50 eV to 30 keV or more, the process has been named “energy dispersive,” although in the spectrometry sense there is no actual dispersion such as occurs in a diffraction element spectrometer. Valid Text Names: 'sramek2026seleniumnanoparticlessmall pages 1-3', 'sramek2026seleniumnanoparticlessmall pages 3-5', 'sramek2026seleniumnanoparticlessmall pages 5-6', 'sramek2026seleniumnanoparticlessmall pages 6-9', 'sramek2026seleniumnanoparticlessmall pages 9-10', 'sramek2026seleniumnanoparticlessmall pages 10-11', 'sramek2026seleniumnanoparticlessmall pages 11-12', 'sramek2026seleniumnanoparticlessmall pages 12-14', 'sramek2026seleniumnanoparticlessmall pages 14-15', 'sramek2026seleniumnanoparticlessmall pages 15-16', 'sramek2026seleniumnanoparticlessmall pages 16-17', 'sramek2026seleniumnanoparticlessmall pages 17-17' BibTex: @article{sramek2026seleniumnanoparticlessmall, author = "Šrámek, Michal and Praus, Lukáš and Benada, Oldřich and Tlustoš, Pavel", title = "Selenium nanoparticles: small innovations with mighty impact on crop performance and nutritional quality?", volume = "13", issn = "2196-5641", url = "https://doi.org/10.1186/s40538-026-00919-x", doi = "10.1186/s40538-026-00919-x", number = "1", journal = "Chemical and Biological Technologies in Agriculture", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC", year = "2026", month = "Jan", issue = "1" } Abstract: Abstract Selenium (Se), a trace element with dual roles as a micronutrient and toxicant, occupies a unique niche in plant physiology and agricultural science. While not essential for plant growth, selenium’s chemical resemblance to sulfur (S) enables its integration into metabolic pathways. This integration influences redox homeostasis, stress resilience, and the nutritional quality of crops. Recent advancements in nanotechnology have unlocked selenium’s latent potential through the use of engineered selenium nanoparticles (SeNPs), primarily zero-valent elemental (Se 0 ) SeNPs. These nanoparticles mitigate the toxicity risks associated with conventional selenite (Se IV O 3 2− ) or selenate (Se VI O 4 2− ) formulations. SeNPs combine enhanced bioavailability with distinctive physicochemical properties. This combination enables enhanced plant growth, stress tolerance, nutrient uptake, and seed quality. Green synthesis methods using plant extracts offer eco-friendly routes to produce stable, biocompatible SeNPs with controlled size and morphology. In crops, SeNPs modulate metabolic pathways and improve photosynthetic pigments. They also synergize with S compounds to boost yield and nutritional content. Additionally, SeNPs contribute to sustainable agriculture by mitigating biotic and abiotic stresses. They enhance food safety through antimicrobial properties in packaging and animal nutrition. Despite their promise, careful dose management is critical due to the narrow therapeutic window of Se and potential toxicity at higher concentrations. This review explores the latest SeNPs synthesis, selenium’s paradoxical role in plant systems, and its agrobiological impacts. Beyond applications, the review identifies critical methodological gaps in existing research, proposes a characterization set for SeNPs studies, and introduces a comprehensive framework for future research priorities. Compositional characterization is essential for understanding and optimizing material performance. For powder-based materials, ubiquitous across diverse technologies, accurately resolving the composition of individual phases at high throughput remains an unsolved challenge. This bottleneck slows material research and is particularly acute for autonomous laboratories, where large numbers of samples are synthesized and AI decision-making algorithms demand low-uncertainty data. Here, we integrate measurement automation, data filtering, and unsupervised machine learning to deliver a fully automated framework for high-throughput, phase-resolved compositional analysis of as-deposited powders using scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDS). Our approach, implemented in the Python-based software AutoEMXSp, overcomes geometry-induced artifacts from irregular particle morphologies and enables accurate compositional quantification using only one experimental standard per element—including light elements conventionally difficult to quantify in powders. Validated across 74 powder samples with elements spanning nitrogen to bismuth, AutoEMXSp consistently estimates compositions within 5–10% of their expected values and resolves minor or intermixed phases with high confidence. By delivering a robust, operator-free, high-throughput framework, this work paves the way for integration of powder compositional characterization into autonomous laboratory platforms, accelerating the pace of materials discovery and development.

"10.3390/pr14020235", number = "2", journal = "Processes", publisher = "MDPI AG", year = "2026", month = "Jan", pages = "235", issue = "2" } Abstract: This study examines the high-temperature degradation of Hastelloy C276, a corrosion-resistant nickel-based alloy, during exposure to combustion products generated by methane and 99% cracked ammonia. Using a high-pressure optical combustor (HPOC) at 4 bar and exhaust temperatures of 815–860 °C, standard tensile specimens were exposed for five hours to fully developed post-flame exhaust gases, simulating real industrial turbine or burner conditions. The surfaces and subsurface regions of the samples were analysed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM; Zeiss Sigma HD FEG-SEM, Carl Zeiss, Oberkochen, Germany) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX; Oxford Instruments X-MaxN detectors, Oxford Instruments, Abingdon, United Kingdom), while mechanical properties were evaluated by tensile testing, and the gas-phase compositions were tracked in detail for each fuel blend. Results show that exposure to methane causes moderate oxidation and some grain boundary carburisation, with localised carbon enrichment detected by high-resolution EDX mapping. In contrast, 99% cracked ammonia resulted in much more aggressive selective oxidation, as evidenced by extensive surface roughening, significant chromium depletion, and higher oxygen incorporation, correlating with increased NOx in the exhaust gas. Tensile testing reveals that methane exposure causes severe embrittlement (yield strength +41%, elongation −53%) through grain boundary carbide precipitation, while cracked ammonia exposure results in moderate degradation (yield strength +4%, elongation −24%) with fully preserved ultimate tensile strength (870 MPa), despite more aggressive surface oxidation. These counterintuitive findings demonstrate that grain boundary integrity is more critical than surface condition for mechanical reliability. These findings underscore the importance of evaluating material compatibility in low-carbon and hydrogen/ammonia-fuelled combustion systems and establish critical microstructural benchmarks for the anticipated mechanical testing in future work. Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The Kulanaokuaiki Tephra Unit 3 (900 C.E.) was a subplinian basaltic scoria eruption, the largest known to have occurred at Kīlauea’s summit. The initiation mechanism and cause(s) of this highly hazardous eruption remain poorly understood, particularly as this style of activity has not been observed in the modern period. We use olivine diffusion timescales from Fe-Mg and lithium zoning to assess magma storage timescales and evaluate evidence for mixing prior to eruption. Of the 200 crystals assessed, 55% are normally zoned for forsterite and 45% are non-zoned. Zoned crystals (> 1 mm) (
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                     = 96) have average compositions of Fo
                    <jats:sub>89</jats:sub>
                    cores and Fo
                    <jats:sub>81</jats:sub>
                    rims, while small crystals 0.5–1 mm (
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                     = 14) have Fo
                    <jats:sub>85</jats:sub>
                    cores and Fo
                    <jats:sub>82</jats:sub>
                    rims. Modeled Fo diffusion timescales range from < 1 to 12.6 years (median of 3.0 years). Lithium maps in 32 of the forsterite-zoned crystals reveal a variety of lithium zoning types, most of which we attribute to crystal growth. Many lithium profiles are coupled to phosphorus within the outer ~ 100 μm of the crystal (
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                     = 17), reflecting growth processes and precluding their use for diffusion studies. Overall, our Unit 3 olivine dataset displays no evidence of magmatic priming shortly prior to eruption, unlike prior observations for the basaltic subplinian eruption of the Keanakāko‘i Tephra Unit E (1650 C.E.). Thus, explosive eruption magmas may be stored for considerably longer than previously thought, and magmatic priming is not a necessary precursor for Kīlauea’s explosive eruptions. We hypothesize that gas-driven filter pressing from crystallization of microlites and macrocrysts in the reservoir slurry contributed to the explosivity of the Unit 3 eruption.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
Abstract 2018 marked the 50th anniversary of the introduction of energy dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS) with semiconductor detectors to electron-excited X-ray microanalysis. Initially useful for qualitative analysis, EDS has developed into a fully quantitative analytical tool that can match wavelength dispersive spectrometry for accuracy in the determination of major (mass concentration C > 0.1) and minor (0.01 ≤ C ≤ 0.1) constituents, and useful accuracy can extend well into the trace (0.001 < C < 0.01) constituent range even when severe peak interference occurs. The excerpt addresses beam current selection and dead-time management as critical aspects of EDS standardization. For Si(Li)-EDS systems, a beam current producing 30% or less dead-time on highly excited pure element standards (Al or Si) is recommended. For more modern SDD-EDS systems, a more conservative approach is advised, keeping dead-time below 10% on the most highly excited standard to minimize coincidence peaks that can affect trace element detection. Crucially, once analytical conditions are established (including EDS time constant, detector solid angle, beam energy, and beam current), these exact conditions must be consistently applied to all standards and unknowns to maintain measurement consistency required for proper k-ratio and matrix correction procedures. This standardization is essential for quantitative accuracy.

Critical parameters for archived standard reuse include maintaining consistency in EDS parameters (detector solid angle, time constant, calibration, window efficiency) and using identical measurement conditions including beam energy, known electron dose (beam current × live-time with dead-time correction), target orientation (ideally 0° tilt), and take-off angle. Surface preparation is essential: specimens require highly polished, flat surfaces with roughness below 100 nm RMS using final polish with 100-nm abrasives; for low-energy photons below 1 keV, surface finish should be better than 50 nm RMS. Chemical polishing should be avoided due to potential compositional changes in the near-surface region sampled by the electron beam. The text emphasizes that consistency in parameter choices is especially critical when using archived standard spectra.

Abstract:
Electron-excited X-ray microanalysis performed in the scanning electron microscope with energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS) is a core technique for characterization of the microstructure of materials. The recent advances in EDS performance with the silicon drift detector (SDD) enable accuracy and precision equivalent to that of the high spectral resolution wavelength-dispersive spectrometer employed on the electron probe microanalyzer platform. SDD-EDS throughput, resolution, and stability provide practical operating conditions for measurement of high-count spectra that form the basis for peak fitting procedures that recover the characteristic peak intensities even for elemental combination where severe peak overlaps occur, such PbS, MoS2, BaTiO3, SrWO4, and WSi2. Accurate analyses are also demonstrated for interferences involving large concentration ratios: a major constituent on a minor constituent (Ba at 0.4299 mass fraction on Ti at 0.0180) and a major constituent on a trace constituent (Ba at 0.2194 on Ce at 0.00407; Si at 0.1145 on Ta at 0.0041). Accurate analyses of low atomic number elements, C, N, O, and F, are demonstrated. Measurement of trace constituents with limits of detection below 0.001 mass fraction (1000 ppm) is possible within a practical measurement time of 500 s.

Abstract:
Measuring the thickness and the composition of precious metal thin films is a challenging task. Currently, the available techniques for thickness measurements are either destructive or need heavy assumptions on the nature of the sample, relying on information that are not always available with sufficient accuracy. In this paper we propose a new methodology based on X-ray microanalysis that can complement, with better lateral resolution, the use of X-ray Fluorescence, the most widely employed technique for measuring the thickness of electrodeposited coatings. The proposed method employs a combination of energy dispersive microanalysis spectra acquisition and Monte Carlo simulation. The effectiveness of the technique has been demonstrated by the measure of the thickness and the composition of a thin 24 kt gold electroplated film that contained small amount of nickel. Results have been validated by comparing data with those obtained by X-ray fluorescence and the scanning electron microscopy of metallographic cross-sections.

The excerpt discusses critical aspects of EDS detector performance and calibration consistency. It emphasizes that energy calibration must be performed consistently before each day's measurements using established protocols to check and recalibrate the detector as needed. The calibration peak position and resolution should remain constant regardless of input count rate or dead-time variations. For accurate quantitative analysis, measured X-ray intensity must scale linearly with effective probe dose—twice the probe dose should produce twice the measured intensity. The text describes validation procedures where intensity divided by probe current should produce a horizontal line when plotted against probe current, indicating proper detector performance. Modern pulse processors typically perform continuous zero offset calibration and adjust electronic gain based on characteristic X-ray features. The excerpt also notes that while modern EDS detectors are highly linear, minor misalignments of KLM markers by a channel or two may occur but need not represent true performance problems.

Abstract:
With lead service lines (LSLs) remaining for decades to come, scale analyses are critical to helping limit lead exposure from drinking water. This laboratory has used an integrated suite of analytical techniques to characterize the elemental composition, mineral identification, and physical features of scales, helping the water industry to evaluate, predict, and reduce lead corrosion. The methods used in this laboratory to prepare and analyze the LSL scale, and guidance to achieving reliable and meaningful results, are described. Primary methods include the following: optical microscopy, powder X‐ray diffraction, inductively coupled plasma spectroscopy, X‐ray fluorescence, scanning electron microscopy with energy dispersive spectroscopy, combustion and coulometric analyses of C and S, and X‐ray absorption spectroscopy. Examples of associated pitfalls and ways to avoid them are provided, including pipe excavation/transport, sample preparation, analysis, and data interpretation. Illustrative examples are presented of practical scale analysis questions that could be answered by combinations of pipe scale analyses.

## 2. Microanalysis and mineralogy of Asian and Saharan dust

Abstract:
Mineral dust is transported over long distances from desert sources, interacting with Earth environments. The mineralogy and microstructures of individual dust particles are required to understand the interactions. Here, I summarize recent findings from electron microscopy of dust particles, focusing on Asian and Saharan dust. Dust particles are heterogeneous mixtures of clay and nonclay minerals. Clay minerals account for more than half of the mass of mineral dust. Fine grains of clay minerals form their own aggregates, coat coarse nonclay minerals, or become a matrix of composite particles. The most abundant clay minerals are illite‒smectite series clay minerals (ISCMs) dominated by illite and interstratified illite‒smectite. Saharan dust is distinct from Asian dust by the high contents of palygorskite and hexagonal kaolinite. Common nonclay silicates are quartz, K-feldspar, and Na-rich plagioclase. Amorphous silica is associated with clays in Saharan dust. Calcite occurs as nanofibers as well as coarse grains, reacting with atmospheric acids to precipitate gypsum. The submicron grains of iron oxides and titanium oxides are scattered through the fine matrix of dust particles. ISCMs, chlorite, biotite, and iron oxides are iron carriers to remote ecosystems. The shapes of dust particles approximate ellipsoids whose aspect ratios increase with clay contents. The mineralogical classification of dust particles has led to the determination of the bulk mineral composition of a very small quantity of samples. The constituent mineralogy of dust particles is discussed in an environmental context with a brief introduction of the geological backgrounds of the minerals in their source areas.

    title = "Systematic compositional analysis of sputter-deposited boron-containing thin films",
    year = "2021",

    month = "Sep",
    doi = "10.1116/6.0001234",
    url = "https://doi.org/10.1116/6.0001234",

    publisher = "American Vacuum Society",
    issue = "6",
    issn = "0734-2101"

Abstract:
Boron-containing materials exhibit a unique combination of ceramic and metallic properties that are sensitively dependent on their given chemical bonding and elemental compositions. However, determining the composition, let alone bonding, with sufficient accuracy is cumbersome with respect to boron, being a light element that bonds in various coordinations. Here, we report on the comprehensive compositional analysis of transition-metal diboride (TMBx) thin films (TM = Ti, Zr, and Hf) by energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDX), x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), time-of-flight elastic recoil detection analysis (ToF-ERDA), Rutherford backscattering spectrometry (RBS), and nuclear reaction analysis (NRA). The films are grown on Si and C substrates by dc magnetron sputtering from stoichiometric TMB2 targets and have hexagonal AlB2-type columnar structures. EDX considerably overestimates B/TM ratios, x, compared to the other techniques, particularly for ZrBx. The B concentrations obtained by XPS strongly depend on the energy of Ar+ ions used for removing surface oxides and contaminants prior to analyses and are more reliable for 0.5 keV Ar+. ToF-ERDA, RBS, and NRA yield consistent compositions in TiBx. They also prove TiBx and ZrBx films to be homogeneous with comparable B/TM ratios for each film. However, ToF-ERDA, employing a 36-MeV 127I8+ beam, exhibits challenges in depth resolution and quantification of HfBx due to plural and multiple scattering and associated energy loss straggling effects. Compared to ToF-ERDA, RBS (for the film grown on C substrates) and NRA provide more reliable B/Hf ratios. Overall, a combination of methods is recommended for accurately pinpointing the compositions of borides that contain heavy transition metals.

Abstract:
A k-ratio is the ratio of a pair of characteristic X-ray line intensities, I, measured under similar experimental conditions for the unknown (unk) and standard (std): 
 
$$ k={I}_{unk}/{I}_{std} $$ 
 
The measured intensities can be associated with a single characteristic X-ray line (as is typically the case for wavelength spectrometers) or associated with a family of characteristic X-ray lines (as is typically the case for energy dispersive spectrometers.) The numerator of the k-ratio is typically the intensity measured from an unknown sample and the denominator is typically the intensity measured from a standard material—a material of known composition.

     Compositional characterization is essential for understanding and optimizing material performance.
     For powder-based materials underpinning many modern technologies, however, accurately and rapidly
      resolving the composition of individual constituent phases remains an unsolved challenge, slowing
      materials research and limiting autonomous laboratory platforms. Scanning electron microscopy with
      energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDS) offers a time- and cost-effective route, but artifacts

1 Introduction

The accelerating pace of materials discovery and optimization is increasingly constrained not by synthesis,
but by the speed and accuracy of characterization—a bottleneck that limits the effectiveness of autonomous,
self-driving laboratories [1–3]. In materials research and development, an essential component of character-
ization is the identification of phases formed during synthesis or processing, including minor or unintended
secondary phases that may affect performance [4–6]. In powder-based materials, foundational to technologies
from energy storage and conversion [7–12] to thermoelectrics [13, 14] and additive manufacturing [15, 16],
crystal structure is typically probed with X-ray diffraction (XRD), but structural data alone are often insuf-
ficient for unambiguous phase identification, particularly in multi-phase or chemically complex systems [17].                   ARTICLE IN PRESS





Complementary compositional analysis is therefore critical, yet established powder characterization meth-
ods are often labor-intensive and fail to simultaneously deliver the quantitative accuracy, throughput, and
spatial resolution needed for rapid phase-level composition analysis across diverse chemistries [6, 18, 19].
   Scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDS) offers an attractive
balance of speed and cost-effectiveness, enabling (sub-)micrometer compositional resolution with min-
imal sample preparation through direct powder deposition onto a substrate [20]. However, in powder
samples, irregular particle sizes and morphologies yield strong mass and absorption effects (see Supplemen-
tary Note 1.1) that significantly distort X-ray peak intensities in EDS spectra, fundamentally compromising
quantification accuracy [20, 21]. This limitation is widespread in commercial SEM-EDS software (see Sup-
plementary Note 1.2), which is typically designed for flat, bulk specimens [21]; when misapplied to particles,
commercial software workflows can produce substantial quantification errors, perpetuating the misconcep-
tion that SEM-EDS is merely a semi-quantitative technique [22]. Nevertheless, the peak-to-background
(P/B) approach offers a way to mitigate geometry-induced artifacts by exploiting the co-localized gener-
ation of peak and continuum X-rays, which scale similarly with particle morphology effects [20, 23]. By
normalizing characteristic peak intensities to the local background, studies have reported relative errors of
10–20% for some micron-scale particle compositions [23–29]. Yet prior demonstrations have been narrow in
scope, typically focusing on a handful of particles and chemistries, and have relied on (1) sample-specific
reference materials—such as strictly compositionally matched standards [24, 25] or standards with a closely
matched average atomic number [23]. Because these methods require a priori knowledge of the sample to
select appropriate references, they are not scalable for analyzing unknown, multiphase reaction products.
Alternatively, prior work has relied on (2) standardless schemes requiring normalization of the measured             PRESSmass fractions to 100% [26–29], which preclude determination of the raw analytical total, a key indicator of
measurement reliability [21, 22, 25]. The absence of an accurate, reliable and scalable quantification scheme,
combined with persistent difficulties in light-element analysis with the P/B method [30], has restricted the         INadoption of SEM-EDS for rigorous phase-level compositional analysis of loose particles dispersed onto a
substrate [22]. As a result, both manual and automated SEM-EDS workflows remain confined to perform-
ing qualitative elemental mapping or broad chemical classification (e.g., aluminosilicates, nitrides) on raw,
unpolished powders [31–33], which is insufficient for accurate phase identification.

quantification using a single experimental standard per element, including light elements conventionally
challenging to quantify in powders. By delivering reliable quantit

2.3 Effectiveness of filtering strategy

attenuation term that avoids overestimation of continuum X-rays at low energies (E < 1 keV) for heavy

with low-energy characteristic X-rays such as N, O and F.

is typically derived from an empirical model for continuum X-ray generation fB, expressed as Bi,b(E) =

critical built-in quality metric for assessing the reliability of the measured composition: a substantial devi-

to standardless quantification approaches.

{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a table summarizing what must be IDENTICAL, what must be RECORDED, and what must be in an ACCEPTABLE RANGE for standards-based SEM-EDS k-ratio quantification when reusing archived standards. This addresses the user's question #4.

Columns: Parameter Category, Parameter, Requirement, Notes/Rationale

MUST BE IDENTICAL between standard and unknown:
- Beam energy (E0) - Must match exactly. Verify by Duane-Hunt limit check.
- EDS detector - Same physical detector
- Pulse process time / time constant - Must be same setting. Controls resolution and throughput.
- Detector-to-specimen distance (solid angle) - Fixed by detector flange typically, but verify working distance is same
- Takeoff angle / detector elevation angle - Fixed by geometry; must match
- Specimen tilt angle - Ideally 0° for both; must be identical if tilted
- Conductive coating scheme - Same material (C), same nominal thickness (<10 nm), especially critical at low kV (5 kV)

MUST BE RECORDED (but need not be identical):
- Probe current (beam current) - Must be measured (Faraday cup or picoammeter) and recorded for each session; used for dose calculation but cancels in k-ratio if dose is properly tracked
- Live time - Must be accurately recorded by dead-time-corrected clock; used with beam current to compute dose
- Acquisition date/time - For traceability and QC tracking

MUST BE IN AN ACCEPTABLE RANGE (but need not be identical):
- Dead time - ≤10% recommended for SDD-EDS quantitative work; ≤5% for trace analysis; need NOT match between standard and unknown
- Input count rate / output count rate - Should produce acceptable dead time; avoid very high rates that cause excessive coincidence
- Spectrum integrated counts - Should be sufficient for desired precision (typically >1 million for major, >10 million for minor/trace)
- Surface roughness - Must be below 50 nm RMS for low-energy photons (<1 keV), below 100 nm RMS for higher energies"}

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Parameter Category | Parameter | Requirement | Notes/Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Must be identical | Beam energy (E0) | Exact same set point for standard and unknown | k-ratio protocol assumes identical excitation conditions; verify actual beam energy from the continuum end point/Duane-Hunt limit as a QC check, especially when reusing archived standards (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000007) |
| Must be identical | EDS detector | Same physical detector | Archived standards are detector-specific because window transmission, solid angle, and response function are part of the measured standard spectrum (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000010) |
| Must be identical | Pulse process time / time constant | Same setting | Time constant controls resolution, peak shape, and throughput; archived standards are only valid if the same processing conditions are used (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000028) |
| Must be identical | Detector-to-specimen distance / effective solid angle | Same geometry; in practice maintain the same working distance and detector position | Measured intensity scales with solid angle; even if the detector flange is fixed, working distance and specimen height must reproduce the archived-standard geometry (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000031) |
| Must be identical | Takeoff angle / detector elevation geometry | Same geometry | X-ray absorption corrections depend on emergence angle, so archived standards should only be reused under the same takeoff geometry (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000031) |
| Must be identical | Specimen tilt angle | Ideally 0° for both; if tilted, tilt must match exactly | Tilt changes path length and absorption; low-tilt, flat geometry is strongly preferred for quantitative work (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000031) |
| Must be identical | Conductive coating scheme | Same coating material and nominal thickness | Coating differences can shift analytical totals and bias k-ratios; for low-kV work (≈5 keV and below) matching coating thickness becomes especially important (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033) |
| Must be recorded | Probe current (beam current) | Measure or otherwise normalize and record for each session | Dose = beam current × live time; absolute current is preferred via Faraday cup/picoammeter, but if unavailable a QC-standard intensity can be used to normalize dose within a verified workflow (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007) |
| Must be recorded | Live time | Record accurately using the dead-time-corrected live-time clock | Dose normalization requires live time, not just real time; intensity should scale linearly with effective dose (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000026) |
| Must be recorded | Acquisition date/time and session metadata | Record for traceability | Needed for archived-standard provenance, long-term QC charts, and troubleshooting drift or maintenance events (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010) |
| Must be in an acceptable range | Dead time | Keep low; about ≤10% recommended for SDD quantitative work, and more conservative for trace work | Dead time does **not** need to be identical between standard and unknown; it must simply stay in a regime where coincidence/pile-up artifacts are negligible and correction remains reliable (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028) |
| Must be in an acceptable range | Input/output count rate | Any rate that preserves stable calibration/resolution and acceptable dead time | Modern SDD systems tolerate high throughput, but very high count rates increase coincidence artifacts; choose rates by detector behavior, not by forcing equality between standard and unknown (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000027) |
| Must be in an acceptable range | Spectrum integrated counts | Sufficient for the target precision | High-count spectra are essential for minor/trace work and robust peak fitting; examples in the literature range from millions to tens of millions of counts depending on problem difficulty (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000025) |
| Must be in an acceptable range | Surface roughness / polish quality | Better than ~100 nm RMS generally; better than ~50 nm RMS for low-energy photons (<1 keV) | Surface topography changes absorption and geometry; low-kV Al/Si/Mg K analysis is especially surface-sensitive, so final polish quality matters directly to k-ratio validity (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032) |


*Table: This table separates conditions that must be strictly matched from those that only need documentation or control within acceptable limits when reusing archived bulk SEM-EDS standards.
